# multimod [<img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="130" alt="multimod website" />](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/)

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/Apache-2.0)
<!-- badges: end -->

> **A unified framework for mathematical model representation, analysis, transformation, and optimization.**

**multimod** is a unified framework for working with mathematical optimization models independently of the languages and solvers used to implement them. Its current implementation is an R package. It represents a model as a structured abstract syntax tree (AST) of sets, mappings, parameters, variables, and equations. That representation can be constructed in R, parsed from supported modeling-language syntax, inspected and transformed, or translated into other representations.

**Define the mathematics once; choose how to express, simplify, and solve it.** Rather than maintaining separate implementations of the same formulation, multimod provides a common model representation and multiple routes from formulation to solution.

## Why multimod?

- **Separate mathematical meaning from implementation.** Work with a structured formulation instead of tying model logic to one programming language, modeling system, or solver.
- **Move between modeling environments.** Generate MathProg, GAMS, JuMP, and Pyomo code, or render equations as LaTeX for inspection and documentation. Import supported subsets of existing GAMS and MathProg models.
- **Avoid unnecessary model-building overhead.** Assemble the linear-programming matrix directly in R and pass it to HiGHS, or export MPS, without first generating and executing another modeling-language implementation.
- **Reduce models to the information their data contains.** Fold dimensions with no variation and trim unused symbols, helping make formulations and their generated representations more compact.
- **Inspect and reuse model structure.** Validate and visualize the AST, examine model statistics, exchange structures as JSON, and maintain data in CSV or Arrow-based workspaces.
- **Support reproducible modeling workflows.** Keep formulations, data, generated code, and solution routes connected through a common model representation.

multimod originated in energy system modeling and includes an energy model among its examples, but **its core is domain-independent**. It can represent linear optimization models in other fields as well.

## Architecture: from formulation to solution

A model can enter multimod through R constructors, supported equation syntax, or a supported source-code reader. Once represented as an AST, it can be inspected, reduced, saved, translated into another modeling language, or compiled directly into an LP matrix. These are alternative routes from the *same mathematical formulation*, not separate models to maintain.

``` text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│      Input Formats          │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ GAMS    (basic/linear only) │ → read_gams()
│ MathProg (limited features) │ → read_gmpl()
│ JuMP    (constraints only)  │ → mm_equation()
│ {{Pyomo, AMPL, MPS, ...}}   │ → {{...}}
└─────────────────────────────┘
              ↓
   ┌────────────────────────┐
   │   multimod Core        │        Analysis & Manipulation:
   │ (Abstract Syntax Tree) │         • fold_model()        [x]
   ├────────────────────────┤         • trim_model()        [x]
   │ • Sets & Aliases       │  →      • save_model()        [x]
   │ • Parameters           │         • as_visNetwork()     [x]
   │ • Variables            │  ←      • model statistics    [x]
   │ • Equations            │         • model_to_json()     [x]
   │ • Mappings             │         {{auto-mapping}}      [ ]
   └────────────────────────┘         {{symbolic simplify}} [ ]
                 ↓                                     ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ Output: model code               │  │ Output: LP matrix                │
├──────────────────────────────────┤  ├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ LaTeX    write_latex()       [x] │  │ model_to_lp()               [x]  │
│ MathProg write_gmpl()        [x] │  │ write_mps()                 [x]  │
│ JuMP     write_jump()        [x] │  │ solve_highs()               [x]  │
│ Pyomo    write_pyomo()       [x] │  │ solve_mps()                 [x]  │
│ GAMS     write_gams() +      [x] │  │ read_mps_solution()         [x]  │
│          write_gams_data()       │  │                                  │
│ {{AMPL, ...}}                [ ] │  │ no generated model text, so      │
│                                  │  │ no model-build step — the        │
│ then an external solver:         │  │ time and memory wall on          │
│ glpsol, Julia, Python, NEOS      │  │ large models                     │
└──────────────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────────────┘

Status: [x] implemented | [~] and { } developing | [ ] and {{ }} considering
```

<!-- ![multimod architecture](man/figures/multimod-architecture.svg) -->

The diagram summarizes the architecture; the table under [Capabilities](#capabilities) lists the implemented functions.

The current tested scope is **linear programming with continuous variables**. Language importers cover documented subsets, and some output routes remain experimental; see [Capabilities](#capabilities) and the [roadmap](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/articles/roadmap.html).

## Installation

```r
pak::pkg_install("optimal2050/multimod")
```

The matrix route requires the 'highs' R package. Other routes require their
corresponding toolchains: `glpsol` (the 'glpsol' R package ships it), Julia
with JuMP, or Python with Pyomo; see the "Configuring solver paths" article.

## Quickstart: one model, several representations

```{r example}
library(multimod)

toy <- example_models$toy          # built in R, see "Writing a model in R"
toy

as_latex(toy$equations$eqDemand)
as_gams(toy$equations$eqDemand)
```

An equation is written as text — MathProg by default, GAMS or JuMP by
choice — and parsed into the same tree the constructors build:

```{r equation}
cap_total <- mm_equation(
  toy,
  "eqCapTotal: sum{t in tech, r in region} vCap[t,r] <= 2000",
  desc = "total installed capacity"
)
as_jump(cap_total, model = toy)
```

The same model solved in R:

```{r solve, eval = requireNamespace("highs", quietly = TRUE)}
r <- solve_highs(toy, attach = FALSE)
r$objective
```

or written for another toolchain and solved there:

```r
ws <- tempfile("toy-"); dir.create(ws)
write_gmpl(toy, model_dir = ws);  solve_gmpl(toy, ws)$objective    # GLPK
write_jump(toy, model_dir = ws);  solve_jump(toy, ws)$objective    # Julia
write_pyomo(toy, model_dir = ws); solve_pyomo(toy, ws, load_results = TRUE)$objective
```

With the documented toolchains and example data, these routes return an objective value of 198000. The "Solving and reading results"
article runs them side by side; "Two models from the field" does the same for
the energyRt reference model and for OSeMOSYS, read from its MathProg source
and solved both through JuMP and from the matrix.

## Capabilities

| | |
|---|---|
| Build a model in R | `new_set()`, `new_parameter()`, `new_variable()`, `new_equation()`, the `ast_*()` expression constructors, `validate()`; `mm_equation()` for an equation written as MathProg, GAMS or JuMP text |
| Read a model | `read_gams()` for the linear subset of GAMS; `read_gmpl()` for MathProg with data sections; `mm_equation(lang = "jump")` for a JuMP `@constraint()` statement |
| Render | `as_gams()`, `as_gmpl()`, `as_jump()`, `as_pyomo()`, `as_latex()` for any node; `write_gams()`, `write_gmpl()`, `write_jump()`, `write_pyomo()`, `write_latex()` for the model |
| Solve in R | `model_to_lp()`, `solve_highs()`, `write_mps()`, `solve_mps()`, `check_matrix_numbers()`, `mm_session()` for repeated solves |
| Solve through generated code | `solve_gmpl()`, `solve_jump()`, `solve_pyomo()`, each loading the solution back |
| Reduce | `fold_model()` drops dimensions a parameter does not vary over; `trim_model()` drops unused symbols |
| Store and exchange | `save_model()`, `load_model()`, `get_data()` (CSV, Arrow IPC, Parquet); `model_to_json()`, `ast_schema()` |

Linear programs with continuous variables are the tested class. Structural model reduction (`fold_model()`, `trim_model()`) is distinct from numerical solver presolving. GAMS output is
readable but not yet runnable without edits, and there is no Pyomo reader; the
[roadmap](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/articles/roadmap.html) lists
what else is not done yet.

## Documentation and next steps

- `vignette("multimod")`: reading, translating, analyzing, exporting and
  solving a model in a few calls.
- [Writing a model in R](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/articles/ast.html): the constructors, step by step.
- [Folding and trimming](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/articles/folding.html): reducing a model to the size
  its data needs.
- Further articles on the [website](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/):
  solving and reading results, the two field models, the model workspace,
  configuration, LaTeX.

## Development direction

The long-term architecture envisages a native C++ or Rust computational core with R and Python interfaces. Future research directions include AI-assisted formulation and support for nonlinear and stochastic optimization. These are planned directions, not implemented features.

The repository is laid out for that architecture: the R package at the root,
`core/` and `python/` reserved for the native core and its Python binding,
`specs/` for the cross-language goldens, and one documentation site under
`docs/` with the R reference at [`/r/`](https://optimal2050.github.io/multimod/r/)
beside the future language sections.

## Integration with energyRt

[energyRt](https://github.com/optimal2050/energyRt) uses multimod as its model
compiler: `energyRt::multimod_from_energyRt()` builds the model from an
interpolated scenario, and the LP or MPS multimod produces is what energyRt
hands to a local solver or, experimentally, to cloud hardware through the
mmcloud package.
